“Well, well, Mr. Bumble,” he said finally, “there’s no denying the coffins have become somewhat narrower and shallower since the new feeding system began. But we have to make a profit, Mr. Bumble. Properly seasoned wood is expensive, sir, and all those iron handles have to come by canal from Birmingham.”

“Well, well,” Mr. Bumble said, “every business has its difficulties. A reasonable profit is perfectly acceptable, of course.”

“Of course it is,” the undertaker replied. “And if I make nothing on one particular item or another, I make up for it in the long run, you understand—he! he! he!”

“Exactly,” said Mr. Bumble.

“Although I must say,” the undertaker continued, returning to the remarks the beadle had interrupted, “I must say, Mr. Bumble, there’s one enormous disadvantage I struggle with: all the fat people die first. Those who were better off, who paid their local taxes for years, are the first to go downhill when they enter the workhouse. And let me tell you, Mr. Bumble, an extra three or four inches beyond your estimate cuts considerably into your profits, especially when you have a family to support, sir.”

Mr. Sowerberry spoke with all the proper indignation of a badly treated man. Mr. Bumble felt that this came rather close to questioning the parish’s honour, and thought a change of subject advisable. Since Oliver Twist was foremost in his thoughts, he began talking about him.

“By the way,” said Mr. Bumble, “you don’t know anyone who needs a boy, do you? A parish apprentice who’s currently a dead weight—a millstone, you might say, around the parish’s neck? Generous terms, Mr. Sowerberry, generous terms.” As he spoke, he raised his cane to the notice overhead and tapped distinctly three times on the words “FIVE POUNDS,” printed in enormous Roman capitals.

“Good heavens!” said the undertaker, taking hold of the gold-edged lapel of Mr. Bumble’s official coat. “That’s exactly what I wanted to discuss with you. You know—my goodness, what an elegant button, Mr. Bumble! I never noticed it before.”

“Yes, I think it’s rather attractive,” the beadle answered, proudly looking down at the large brass buttons decorating his coat. “The design is the same as the parish seal—the Good Samaritan tending the sick and wounded man. The board gave it to me on New Year’s morning, Mr. Sowerberry. I remember wearing it for the first time to the inquest on that tradesman who had fallen into poverty and died in a doorway at midnight.”

Elizabeth gave herself no time to think. Scarcely knowing what she felt, she finished the letter, immediately grabbed the other, and opened it with desperate impatience. It had been written a day after the first was finished, and she read:

“My dearest sister, by now you have received my hurried letter. I hope this one will be easier to understand. I have more time to write, but my thoughts are so confused that I cannot promise to make sense. Dearest Lizzy, I hardly know what to say, but I have bad news, and you must hear it at once. However unwise a marriage between Mr. Wickham and poor Lydia would be, we now long for proof that they are married. There is far too much reason to fear they have not gone to Scotland. Colonel Forster arrived yesterday. He left Brighton the previous day, only a few hours after the urgent message was sent. Lydia’s brief letter to Mrs. F. suggested they were going to Gretna Green. But Denny made a remark saying he believed W. had never meant to go there, or to marry Lydia at all. When this reached Colonel F., he became alarmed and immediately left Brighton to follow their route. He easily traced them as far as Clapham, but there the trail ended. On reaching that place, they changed to a hired town coach and sent away the carriage that had brought them from Epsom. All we know after that is that someone saw them continue along the London road. I do not know what to think. Colonel F. asked everywhere he could on that side of London, then continued into Hertfordshire. He anxiously questioned people again at every tollgate and at the inns in Barnet and Hatfield, but without success. No one had seen a couple like them passing through. With the kindest concern, he came on to Longbourn and told us his fears with a tenderness that did him great credit. I feel deeply sorry for him and Mrs. F., though no one can blame them. We are terribly distressed, dear Lizzy. Father and Mother believe the worst, but I cannot think so badly of him. Many things might make a quiet marriage in London more convenient than their original plan. And even if he could mean to treat a young woman from Lydia’s family in such a way—which seems unlikely—can I believe she has abandoned every principle? Impossible! Sadly, though, Colonel F. has little confidence that they will marry. When I spoke of my hopes he shook his head, saying he feared W. could not be trusted.”

“‘We called at your home,’ said the first man, ‘and unfortunately did not find you there. We were told you had probably walked this way, so we followed, hoping to catch up with you. Please get into the carriage.’

“Both men spoke and acted as though they expected obedience. While these words were being said, they moved so that I stood between them and the carriage door. They carried weapons. I had none.

“‘Gentlemen,’ I said, ‘forgive me, but I generally ask who wishes to consult me, and what sort of case requires my help.’

“The man who had spoken second answered me. ‘Doctor, your patients are people of high rank. As for the case itself, we trust your skill to discover its nature better than we could explain it. That is enough. Please get into the carriage.’

“I had no choice but to obey, and stepped inside without another word. They followed me, the last man folding up the steps before jumping in. The carriage turned and drove off as fast as before.

“I have repeated this conversation exactly as it happened. I am certain the words are the same. I describe every event precisely, forcing my thoughts to remain on this task. At the broken marks I put here, I stop writing for the present and return this paper to its hiding place.

“The carriage left the streets, passed through the North Barrier, and came out onto the country road. Two-thirds of a league beyond the Barrier, it turned off the main road and soon stopped at an isolated house. I did not judge the distance then; I learned it later when I travelled the route again. All three of us got out. We followed a soft, wet garden path to the door, passing a neglected fountain that had overflowed. No one answered the bell immediately. When a man finally opened the door, one of my escorts struck him across the face with his heavy riding glove.

“The blow itself did not particularly catch my attention. I had seen ordinary people beaten more often than dogs. But the second man was angry too, and struck the servant in the same way with his arm. At that moment the brothers’ faces and manner were so alike that I realized for the first time they were twins.

“Ever since we had got out at the outer gate, I had heard cries from an upstairs room. That gate had been locked; one of the brothers opened it to let us in, then locked it behind us.”
